title: The structure and function of the feet
intro: The feet carry your whole body weight, absorb shock and propel you forward with every step. Each foot has 26 bones, many joints, strong ligaments, tendons and muscles that work together. Understanding how the foot is built helps explain common problems and how to care for them.

sections.heading: Bones and joints
paragraphs: The foot has three main regions: the hindfoot with the heel bone and ankle bone, the midfoot with several smaller bones forming the arch, and the forefoot with the five long bones and the toes. The big toe has two bones and the other toes three. Joints between them allow the foot to adapt to uneven ground and to stiffen when pushing off.

sections.heading: Arches
paragraphs: The foot forms arches along its length and across its width. These act like springs, spreading the load and absorbing shock. Flat feet have lower arches and high arches are more rigid. Both can be normal and cause no problems, but may sometimes lead to pain or fatigue.

sections.heading: Ligaments, tendons and muscles
paragraphs: Ligaments connect bones and stabilise joints. The plantar fascia, a thick band under the foot, supports the arch. Tendons connect muscles of the lower leg and the foot to bones, like the Achilles tendon, the strongest in the body, linking calf muscles to the heel. Small muscles in the foot control the toes and support the arch.

sections.heading: Skin, nerves and circulation
paragraphs: The sole has thick skin and a fat pad under the heel and ball that cushion impact. Nerves provide the sense of touch and balance, and blood vessels deliver oxygen. Reduced sensation or circulation, as in diabetes, makes injury and infection more likely.

sections.heading: Caring for your feet
paragraphs: Wear well-fitting shoes with space for the toes and good support, change them regularly, and avoid high heels for long periods. Walk barefoot on safe surfaces to strengthen foot muscles, keep the skin clean and moisturised, trim nails straight and check feet regularly. Persistent pain, deformity or changes in skin and nails should be assessed.

examples.title: Choosing shoes
examples.text: Imagine you shop for new walking shoes. You could try them on in the afternoon, check that your toes can wiggle freely and walk around the shop before buying.

examples.title: Strengthening the foot
examples.text: Suppose your arches feel tired after long standing. You might practise picking up a towel with your toes and rolling your foot on a ball for a few minutes daily.
